danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 1
paragraphs: Efter fyrst Andrejs forlovelse med Natasja følte Pierre pludselig og uden nogen klar årsag, at det var umuligt at fortsætte med at leve som før. Så overbevist han end var om de sandheder, hans velgører havde åbenbaret for ham, og så lykkelig han end havde været med at fuldkommengøre sit indre menneske, som han med så stor iver havde viet sig til — al glæden ved et sådant liv forsvandt efter Andrejs og Natasjas forlovelse og Joseph Aleksejevitjs død, nyheden om hvilken nåede ham næsten samtidig. Kun livets skelet var tilbage: hans hus, en strålende hustru, der nu nød en meget betydningsfuld persons gunst, bekendtskab med hele Petersborg og hans hoftjeneste med dens kedelige formaliteter. Og dette liv forekom Pierre pludselig uventet modbydelig. Han holdt op med at skrive dagbog, undgik brødrenes selskab, begyndte at gå i klubben igen, drak en del og kom atter i berøring med ungkarlekredse, og førte et sådant liv, at grevinde Hélène fandt det nødvendigt at tale strengt til ham om det. Pierre følte, at hun havde ret, og for at undgå at kompromittere hende rejste han til Moskva.

I Moskva følte han sig straks hjemme, så snart han trådte ind i sit enorme hus, hvor de falme og falmende prinsesser stadig boede, med dets vældige følge; så snart han, kørende gennem byen, så Iberskhelligdommen med utallige lys brændende foran ikonernes gyldne indfatninger, Kreml-pladsen med sin uberørte sne, droskekuskene og hytterne i Sivtsev Vrazjok, de gamle moskovitter, der intet ønskede, ingen steder skyndte sig og gled fredeligt mod livets afslutning; da han så de gamle moskva-damer, Moskvas baller og den Engelske Klub, følte han sig hjemme i en rolig havn. I Moskva følte han sig i fred, hjemme, varm og beskidt som i en gammel morgenkappe.

Moskvas selskab, fra de gamle kvinder til børnene, modtog Pierre som en længe ventet gæst, hvis plads altid stod parat og ventede på ham. For Moskvas selskabsliv var Pierre den venligste, mest godmodige, mest intelligente, muntreste og gavmildeste af alle sære eksistenser, en sorgløs, godsindet adelsmand af den gamle russiske type. Hans pengepung var altid tom, fordi den stod åben for enhver.

Velgørenhedsforestillinger, dårlige malerier, statuer, velgørende selskaber, sigøjnerkor, skoler, middage på abonnement, drikkegilderne, frimurerne, kirker og bøger — ingen og intet mødte afslag fra ham, og havde det ikke været for to venner, der havde lånt store summer af ham og taget ham under deres beskyttelse, ville han have givet alt væk. Der var aldrig en middag eller soiré i klubben uden ham. Så snart han sank ned på sin plads på sofaen efter to flasker Margaux, blev han omringet, og snak, diskussion og vittigheder begyndte. Når der var skærmydsler, forsonede hans venlige smil og velanbragte spøg de stridende. Frimurermiddagene var kedelige og triste, når han ikke var der.

Når han efter et ungkarlegilde rejste sig med sit elskværdige og venlige smil og bøjede sig for det festlige selskabs opfordringer til at køre et sted hen med dem, lød jubelråb blandt de unge mænd. Til baller dansede han, hvis der manglede en partner. De unge damer, gifte som ugifte, holdt af ham, for uden at kurtisere nogen af dem var han lige elskværdig over for alle, især efter souperen. »Il est charmant; il n'a pas de sexe,«* sagde de om ham.
* »Han er charmerende; han har intet køn.«
Pierre var en af disse pensionerede kammerjunkere, som der var hundredvis af, der hyggede sig igennem deres dage i Moskva.

Hvor forfærdet ville han ikke have været syv år tidligere, da han først kom hjem fra udlandet, hvis nogen havde fortalt ham, at der ikke var behov for, at han søgte eller planlagde noget, at hans spor for længst var lagt, evigt forudbestemt, og at han, hvor meget han end spjættede, ville blive det, alle i hans stilling blev. Ville han ikke have troet det! Havde han ikke på ét tidspunkt af hele sit hjerte længtes efter at oprette en republik i Rusland; så selv at blive en Napoleon; så at blive filosof; og så strateg og Napoleons besejrer? Havde han ikke set muligheden for og lidenskabeligt ønsket hele den syndige menneskeracens genrejsning og sin egen opstigning til den højeste grad af fuldkommenhed? Havde han ikke oprettet skoler og hospitaler og frigivet sine livegne?

Men i stedet for alt det — her sad han, den rige ægtemand til en utro hustru, en pensioneret kammerjunker, der holdt af at spise og drikke og, mens han knappede vesten op, at skælde lidt ud over regeringen, et medlem af Moskvas Engelske Klub og en alles yndling i Moskvas selskabsliv. I lang tid kunne han ikke forsone sig med tanken om, at han var en af de samme pensionerede moskovitiske kammerjunkere, som han havde foragtet syv år tidligere.

Somme tider trøstede han sig med den tanke, at han kun levede dette liv midlertidigt; men så blev han forskrækket over tanken om, hvor mange der, ligesom han, havde trådt ind i det liv og den klub midlertidigt, med alle deres tænder og alt deres hår, og først havde forladt det, da ikke en eneste tand eller et eneste hår var tilbage.

I stunder af stolthed, når han tænkte over sin stilling, forekom det ham, at han var helt anderledes og adskilt fra de andre pensionerede kammerjunkere, han tidligere havde foragtet: de var tomme, dumme, tilfredse fyre, tilfredse med deres position, »mens jeg stadig er utilfreds og vil gøre noget for menneskeheden. Men måske kæmpede alle disse mine lidelsesfæller ligesom jeg og søgte noget nyt, en egen vej i livet, og blev ligesom mig af omstændighedernes, samfundets og racens magt — af den elementære kraft, mennesket er magtesløst overfor — bragt til den tilstand, jeg befinder mig i,« sagde han til sig selv i stunder af ydmyghed; og efter at have boet i Moskva i nogen tid foragtede han ikke længere, men begyndte at holde af, at respektere og at have medlidenhed med sine skæbnefæller, ligesom han havde medlidenhed med sig selv.

Pierre led ikke længere af anfald af fortvivlelse, tungsind og livslede, men den sygdom, der tidligere havde fundet udløb i sådanne akutte anfald, var trængt indad og forlod ham aldrig et øjeblik. »Hvorfor? Hvorfor? Hvad foregår der i verden?« spurgte han sig selv i forvirring flere gange om dagen, idet han ufrivilligt begyndte at grunde over livets fænomeners mening; men da han af erfaring vidste, at der ikke var svar på disse spørgsmål, skyndte han sig at vende sig bort fra dem og tog en bog op eller skyndte sig til klubben eller til Apollon Nikolajevitj for at udveksle byens sladder.

»Hélène, der aldrig har interesseret sig for andet end sin egen krop og er en af verdens dummeste kvinder,« tænkte Pierre, »anses af folk for toppunktet af intelligens og forfinelse, og de hylder hende. Napoleon Bonaparte blev foragtet af alle, så længe han var stor, men nu da han er blevet en ynkelig komiker, vil kejser Frans tilbyde ham sin datter i et ulovligt ægteskab. Spanierne priser gennem den katolske gejstlighed Gud for deres sejr over franskmændene den fjortende juni, og franskmændene priser ligeledes gennem den katolske gejstlighed Gud, fordi de den selvsamme fjortende juni besejrede spanierne. Mine frimurerbrødre sværger ved blodet, at de er rede til at ofre alt for deres næste, men de giver ikke en rubel hver til indsamlingerne for de fattige, og de intrigerer, Astræa-logen mod Manna-søgerne, og gør vrøvl om et autentisk skotsk tæppe og et charter, som ingen har brug for, og hvis mening den selvsamme mand, der skrev det, ikke forstår. Vi bekender os alle til den kristne lov om tilgivelse af uret og kærlighed til vor næste, den lov, til hvis ære vi har bygget fyrre gange fyrre kirker i Moskva — men i går blev en desertør pisket til døde, og en forkynder af den selvsamme kærlighedens og tilgivelsens lov, en præst, gav soldaten et kors at kysse før henrettelsen.« Sådan tænkte Pierre, og hele dette almene bedrag, som alle accepterer, forbløffede ham, vant som han var til det, hver gang som var det noget nyt. »Jeg forstår bedraget og forvirringen,« tænkte han, »men hvordan skal jeg fortælle dem alle, hvad jeg ser? Jeg har prøvet og har altid fundet, at de også, i bunden af deres sjæle, forstår det som jeg, og blot prøver ikke at se det. Sådan forekommer det altså at måtte være! Men jeg — hvad skal der blive af mig?« tænkte han. Han havde den ulykkelige evne, mange mennesker, især russere, har, til at se og tro på muligheden af godhed og sandhed, men at se livets ondskab og falskhed for tydeligt til at kunne tage alvorlig del i det. Enhver virkekreds var i hans øjne forbundet med ondskab og bedrag. Hvad han end forsøgte at være, hvad han end engagerede sig i, frastødte det ondes og falskes ham og spærrede enhver vej til virksomhed. Og dog måtte han leve og finde beskæftigelse. Det var for frygteligt at bære byrden af disse uløselige problemer, så han hengav sig til enhver adspredelse for at glemme dem. Han opsøgte enhver form for selskab, drak meget, købte malerier, kastede sig ud i byggerier og frem for alt — læste.

Han læste, og læste alt hvad der faldt ham i hænderne. Når han kom hjem og kammerherrerne endnu var i gang med at klæde ham af, greb han en bog og begyndte at læse. Fra læsning gik han over til at sove, fra at sove til sladder i saloner og klubben, fra sladder til drikkegilderne og kvinder; fra drikkegilderne tilbage til sladder, læsning og vin. Drikkeriet blev mere og mere en fysisk og også moralsk nødvendighed. Selvom lægerne advarede ham om, at med hans fedme var vin farlig, drak han en hel del. Han følte sig først rigtigt tilpas, når han mekanisk havde hældt adskillige glas vin i sin store mund og mærkede en behagelig varme i kroppen, en venlighed over for alle sine medmennesker og en parathed til overfladisk at reagere på enhver idé uden at gå den i dybden. Først efter at have tømt en flaske eller to fornemmede han dunkelt, at livets frygteligt sammenfiltrede nøgle, der tidligere havde forfærdet ham, ikke var så forfærdelig, som han havde troet. Han var altid bevidst om et eller andet aspekt af det nøgle, mens han med summen i hovedet efter middag eller souper snakkede, lyttede til samtale eller læste. Men under vinens indflydelse sagde han til sig selv: »Det gør ikke noget. Jeg skal nok rede det ud. Jeg har en løsning parat, men har ikke tid nu — det tænker jeg over senere!« Men det »senere« kom aldrig.
Om morgenen, på tom mave, stod alle de gamle spørgsmål lige så uløselige og forfærdelige som altid, og Pierre greb hastigt en bog, og hvis nogen kom på besøg, var han glad.

Undertiden huskede han, hvordan han havde hørt, at soldater i krig, når de ligger i skyttegrave under fjendtlig ild og intet har at bestille, ihærdigt søger en beskæftigelse for lettere at udholde faren. For Pierre forekom alle mennesker som disse soldater, der søgte tilflugt fra livet: nogle i ærgerrighed, nogle i kort, nogle i at lave love, nogle i kvinder, nogle i legetøj, nogle i heste, nogle i politik, nogle i sport, nogle i vin og nogle i statslige anliggender. »Intet er trivielt, og intet er vigtigt, det er alt det samme — bare at redde sig fra det, så godt man kan,« tænkte Pierre. »Blot ikke at se det, det forfærdelige det!«

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 1
paragraphs: After Prince Andrew's engagement to Natasha, Pierre suddenly felt — without any apparent reason — that it was impossible to go on living as before. Firmly convinced as he was of the truths revealed to him by his benefactor, and happy as he had been in perfecting his inner self, to which he had devoted himself with such passion — all the meaning of such a life vanished after Andrew's engagement and the death of Joseph Alexeevich, the news of which reached him almost simultaneously. Only the skeleton of life remained: his house, a brilliant wife who now enjoyed the favors of a very important personage, acquaintance with all of Petersburg, and his court service with its dull formalities. And this life suddenly seemed unbearably loathsome to Pierre. He stopped keeping a diary, avoided the Brothers, began going to the club again, drank heavily, and fell back in with the bachelor crowd, leading such a life that Countess Helene thought it necessary to scold him severely about it. Pierre felt she was right, and to avoid embarrassing her he left for Moscow.

In Moscow, as soon as he entered his huge house where the faded and aging princesses still lived with their enormous household; as soon as he drove through the city and saw the Iberian shrine with its countless candles burning before the golden icon covers, the Kremlin Square with its undisturbed snow, the cabbies and hovels of the Sivtsev Vrazhok — those old Muscovites who wanted nothing, hurried nowhere, and were peacefully living out their days; when he saw the old Moscow ladies, the Moscow balls, and the English Club — he felt himself at home in a quiet haven. In Moscow he felt at peace, at home, warm and slovenly as in an old dressing gown.

Moscow society, from the grandmothers down to the children, received Pierre like a long-awaited guest whose place was always ready and waiting. For Moscow society Pierre was the nicest, kindest, smartest, jolliest, and most generous of eccentrics — a heedless, good-natured nobleman of the old Russian type. His purse was always empty because it was open to everyone.

Benefit concerts, bad paintings, statues, charitable societies, gypsy choirs, schools, subscription dinners, drinking bouts, Freemasons, churches, and books — nothing and no one ever met with a refusal from him, and if it hadn't been for two friends who had borrowed large sums and taken him under their wing, he would have given everything away. There was never a dinner or soiree at the club without him. As soon as he sank into his spot on the sofa after two bottles of Margaux, people gathered around and the talking, arguing, and joking began. When quarrels broke out, his kindly smile and well-timed jokes reconciled the opponents. The Masonic dinners were dreary and dull when he wasn't there.

When, after a bachelor supper, he got up with his amiable, kindly smile and yielded to entreaties to go off somewhere with the revelers, shouts of delight and triumph arose among the young men. At balls he danced whenever a partner was needed. Young ladies, married and unmarried, liked him because he was equally friendly to all without making love to any of them, especially after supper. "He's charming; he has no sex," they said of him.
* "He is charming; he has no sex."
Pierre was one of those hundreds of retired gentlemen-in-waiting who were good-naturedly living out their days in Moscow.

How horrified he would have been seven years earlier, when he first came back from abroad, if someone had told him there was no need for him to seek or plan anything, that his groove had long been carved, predetermined from eternity, and that no matter how he wriggled he would become what everyone in his position became. He could not have believed it! Hadn't he once longed with all his heart to establish a republic in Russia; then to be a Napoleon; then a philosopher; then a strategist and the conqueror of Napoleon? Hadn't he seen the possibility of, and passionately desired, the regeneration of sinful humanity and his own rise to the highest perfection? Hadn't he established schools and hospitals and freed his serfs?

But instead of all that — here he was, the wealthy husband of an unfaithful wife, a retired gentleman-in-waiting, fond of eating and drinking and of — as he unbuttoned his waistcoat — grumbling about the government; a member of the Moscow English Club and a universal favorite in Moscow society. For a long time he couldn't reconcile himself to the idea that he had become one of those very same retired Moscow gentlemen-in-waiting he had so despised seven years ago.

Sometimes he consoled himself with the thought that he was only living this way temporarily; but then he was startled by the realization that how many others, like him, had entered this life and this club "temporarily" — with a full head of teeth and hair — and had only left when not a single tooth or hair remained.

In moments of pride, when he reflected on his position, it seemed to him that he was quite different from and distinct from those other retired gentlemen-in-waiting he had formerly looked down on: they were empty, stupid, self-satisfied fellows, content with their lot, "while I am still dissatisfied and want to do something for humanity. But perhaps all these comrades of mine struggled just as I did, looking for something new, a path of their own — and like me were brought by force of circumstances, of society, of upbringing, by that elemental force against which man is powerless, to the same state I'm in," he told himself in moments of humility. And after living in Moscow for a while he no longer despised but began to grow fond of, respect, and pity his fellows in fate, just as he pitied himself.

Pierre no longer suffered those acute bouts of despair, self-loathing, and disgust with life. But the same illness that had once expressed itself in those violent attacks was now driven inward and never left him for a moment. "What for? Why? What is going on in the world?" he would ask himself several times a day, perplexed, involuntarily starting to ponder the meaning of things anew. But knowing from experience that there were no answers to these questions, he quickly turned away from them and picked up a book, or hurried off to the club or to Apollon Nikolaevich's to swap the latest gossip.

"Helene, who has never cared about anything except her own body and is one of the stupidest women alive," thought Pierre, "is regarded by people as the pinnacle of intelligence and refinement, and they worship her. Napoleon Bonaparte was despised by everyone as long as he was great, but now that he has become a pathetic comedian, Emperor Francis wants to offer him his daughter in an illegal marriage. The Spaniards, through the Catholic clergy, offer thanks to God for their victory over the French on the fourteenth of June — and the French, also through the Catholic clergy, give thanks for defeating the Spaniards on that same fourteenth of June. My brother Masons swear by their blood that they are ready to sacrifice everything for their neighbor, but they won't give a ruble each to charity, and they scheme — the Astraea Lodge against the Manna Seekers — and fuss over an authentic Scottish carpet and a charter that nobody needs and whose very author doesn't understand. We all profess the Christian law of forgiving injuries and loving our neighbors — the law in whose honor we've built forty times forty churches in Moscow — but yesterday a deserter was flogged to death, and a minister of that same law of love and forgiveness gave the soldier a cross to kiss before his execution." So thought Pierre, and this whole universal deception — which everyone accepted, accustomed as they were to it — astonished him afresh each time, as if it were something new. "I see the deception and confusion," he thought, "but how am I to tell them all that I see? I have tried, and I've always found that they too, deep in their souls, understand it as I do — they just try not to look. So it seems this is how things must be! But I — what is to become of me?" he thought. He had the unfortunate capacity — common among men, especially Russians — of seeing and believing in the possibility of goodness and truth, but of seeing the evil and falsehood of life too clearly to be able to take any serious part in it. Every sphere of activity was connected, in his eyes, with evil and deception. Whatever he tried to be, whatever he took up, the evil and falsehood repelled him and blocked every path. Yet he had to live and find something to do. It was too terrible to exist under the burden of these unsolvable problems, so he abandoned himself to every distraction in order to forget them. He went everywhere, drank a great deal, bought paintings, took up construction, and above all — read.

He read, and read everything that came to hand. On coming home, while his valets were still helping him undress, he would pick up a book and start reading. From reading he passed to sleeping, from sleeping to gossip at drawing rooms and the club, from gossip to drinking and women, from drinking back to gossip, reading, and wine. Drinking became more and more both a physical and a moral necessity. Though the doctors warned him that wine was dangerous for someone of his weight, he drank heavily. He only felt fully at ease when, having mechanically poured several glasses of wine into his large mouth, he felt a pleasant warmth in his body, an amiability toward everyone, and a readiness to respond to any idea without probing it too deeply. Only after a bottle or two did he feel dimly that the terribly tangled skein of life that had previously horrified him was not as dreadful as he had thought. He was always vaguely aware of some thread of that skein, buzzing in his head after dinner or supper, while chatting, listening, or reading. But under the influence of wine he would tell himself: "It doesn't matter. I'll untangle it. I have a solution worked out, but I don't have time right now — I'll think it all through later." But the "later" never came.
In the morning, on an empty stomach, all the old questions looked as insoluble and terrible as ever, and Pierre hastily picked up a book. And if someone came to visit, he was glad.

Sometimes he recalled how he had heard that soldiers in war, when trapped under enemy fire with nothing to do, try hard to find some occupation to make it easier to bear the danger. To Pierre, all people seemed like those soldiers, seeking refuge from life: some in ambition, some in cards, some in lawmaking, some in women, some in toys, some in horses, some in politics, some in sport, some in wine, some in government affairs. "Nothing is trivial and nothing is important — it's all the same — only to escape from it as best one can," thought Pierre. "Only not to see it — that dreadful it!"
